links.outcome: Frequency of clinician edits to ambient AI note content (facts, orders, symptoms, medications, diagnoses)
links.effect: Most edited content was clinical facts: orders 40.0%, symptoms 30.3%, medication prescriptions 27.3%, diagnosis descriptions 25.9%; terminology edits 11.6%, language style 7.2%.
links.quote: The most frequently edited content pertained to clinical facts including orders (eg, procedures, lab tests) (40.0%), symptoms (30.3%), medication prescriptions (27.3%), and diagnosis descriptions (25.9%).

links.outcome: Need for specialty-specific detail edits in ambient AI drafts
links.effect: Thematic analysis found clinicians edited drafts to add medical specialty-specific details, one of 5 main edit types, indicating generic drafts fit specialties poorly.
links.quote: The results of our thematic analysis show that most edits can be categorized into one of the following 5 types: to revise factual discrepancies, to add medical specialty-specific details, to express diagnostic certainties, to convert patient expressions into objective assessments recorded in medical terms, and to reorganize or condense content.

screen.reason: Analyzed clinician edits on real-world ambient AI-drafted documentation from 200 clinical encounters to determine what clinicians modify, directly measuring the role and effectiveness of human clinician review as a deployment safeguard.

primary.practice: clinician review and editing of AI-drafted documentation
